1:
Barnes and Clarke agree that the verse is in the wrong chapter, both holding that it belongs with the promises quoted at the close of the previous one and should have been joined to them; Wesley places it as the second half of an exhortation proposed earlier and resumed a few verses back. What those promises are then divides two men of the same school. Gill insists they were held not in hope, as older saints held the promise of a Messiah and later ones the resurrection, but in hand and in actual possession, since God had already become their God and Father; and he presses the point that these are absolute and unconditional blessings, which he takes as clear proof that a covenant of that kind has no tendency to licentiousness but the contrary. Calvin argues the opposite way from the same verse. God does anticipate us by his pure favour, but having conferred it he requires gratitude in return, and in every promise a condition is tacitly appended, so that the promises call us to sanctification as if God had interposed by an implied agreement. Barnes reads the exhortation simply as a call to make every effort after perfect purity.

The two kinds of filthiness are given very different contents. Clarke is concrete about both, taking the first for drunkenness, fornication and the sins done immediately against the body, and the second for impure desires, unholy thoughts and polluting imaginations; Wesley divides them simply as all outward sin and all inward. Robertson works from the word, a late one meaning to stain or pollute, found in the Greek Bible and in Plutarch and Josephus, and holds that it takes in filthiness of every kind, physical, moral, mental and ceremonial; he remarks that missionaries in the East can appreciate the atmosphere of pollution at Corinth. Ellicott narrows it instead. The noun occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, is used elsewhere of the pollution of idolatry and of the sin of Sodom, and its cognate verb of sexual impurity, so that idolatry and impurity were blended inextricably in the apostle's mind; having warned against the feasts held in idol temples he could not shut his eyes to what accompanied them, and Ellicott names the Roman satirists as showing what defilement of the spirit meant. Calvin uses the pair polemically, arguing that if inward superstition is a defilement of the spirit, those who excuse outward idolatry on pretexts have left themselves nothing to call defilement of the flesh.

On the last clause the commentators are careful that it not be read as a finished state. Robertson makes the grammar carry it, noting the present tense and calling this not merely the negative goodness of cleansing but something aggressive and progressive, a continuous process rather than a sudden attainment; he also observes that Paul includes himself in the exhortation rather than standing outside it. Wesley makes the same point in his own idiom, that we are not to rest in a negative religion but to carry holiness to its height in all its branches and endure to the end. Henry sets the standard higher still and concedes at once that it cannot be reached: we must be still perfecting holiness and not content ourselves with sincerity, which is our gospel perfection, but aim at sinless perfection, though we shall always come short of it while we are in this world. He also ties the clause back to the promises, since if we hope God is our Father we must endeavour to partake of his holiness. Calvin insists the demand reaches the visible man, so that we are to be pure not only in defilements which God alone witnesses but in those that fall under the observation of others.
2:
The request itself is read as a plea rather than a command. Robertson gives the verb its plain sense, to leave a space or make room, and notes that Paul wants no further tightness of heart in them and addresses even the stubborn minority. Ellicott hears an almost infinite pathos in it, and reconstructs the undercurrent: having complained that they were straitened in their affections, and thinking now of the party of licence and what their companionship with idolaters exposed them to, he entreats almost with sobs, as though asking whether men who could find room for such as those have none for him. Chrysostom notices the word chosen and why. Paul does not say love us, but uses the phrase that appeals more strongly to pity, and asks a favour that carries no burden and profits the giver more than the receiver; and, having convicted them of loving less than they were loved, he softens the rebuke by asking for what he had just reproached them for withholding. Calvin puts the same request in terms of doctrine, that they should not let corrupt affections or unfavourable apprehensions keep his teaching from finding a place in them, since it would be unseemly for a man labouring with a father's zeal to be telling a story to the deaf.

The three denials are taken as a list with distinct heads. Wesley separates them most crisply, that Paul had hurt no man in his person, corrupted none in his principles and defrauded none of his property, adding that he intimates the good he had done with the utmost modesty, as though not looking at it. Calvin names the same three as the faults by which pastors commonly alienate their people, an overbearing use of authority, the corrupting of those they should have guided with false doctrine, and an insatiable desire for what belongs to another. Robertson translates the second as ruining, and reports another commentator's view that it may refer to money, morals or doctrine. Clarke and Gill both see the denial pointed elsewhere: Clarke lists what the false teachers had done in contrast, beguiling them from the simplicity of the truth, bringing them into bondage, devouring them and exalting themselves, all patiently suffered; Gill insists the clearing of himself is not meant to accuse them but to distinguish him from those men. Barnes suggests instead that some may have thought themselves injured by the sternness of his requirements, whether in forbidding alliances with unbelievers or in the discipline of the incestuous person, and that all of it was the fruit of tender love.

On the disclaimer that follows, Ellicott finds a sudden revulsion of feeling: there is no you in the Greek and the vagueness seems intentional, and what had sounded like a reproach is swallowed up as the recollection of Titus's news rushes back. Calvin admires the restraint. The Corinthians deserved to be made the guilty party once Paul was acquitted, on two counts, ingratitude and calumny, yet he refrains from recrimination and stands simply on the defensive, since those who love do not assail but either cover a fault or soften it, a disposition to reproach being a sign of hatred. Clarke and Ellicott independently reach for the same ode of Horace to gloss the pledge to die and live together, Clarke adding that there was never a church less worthy of an apostle's affection and none more beloved. On the overflowing joy of the last verse, Clarke and Robertson converge again on the rarity of the verb, Clarke saying he has not met it in any Greek author and Robertson that outside this place it appears only in Byzantine writers and means to have a regular flood. Calvin reads the three clauses as a climax, boldness rising to glorying and glorying to a joy that dispels the grief many heavy afflictions had caused.
5:
Everyone notices that Paul has resumed a thread dropped four chapters earlier. Ellicott, Robertson, Henry and Barnes all connect the words about Macedonia to the moment at Troas where he said he had no rest in his spirit, and Ellicott points out that the earlier phrase was about the spirit while this one is about the flesh, so that his body was still suffering want of rest even after his mind had steadied. Robertson makes the grammar carry the disorder, noting the dramatic perfect, an anacoluthon where the participle agrees with neither case before it, and a parenthesis with no connecting particle in the clause about fightings and fears. Calvin reads the same construction as a deliberate limit: in saying his flesh had no rest Paul is saying that as a man he had no relief, excepting the spiritual consolations by which he was meanwhile sustained. Clarke fixes the itinerary, from Ephesus to Troas and then to Macedonia, from which the letter was written, and Gill notes that he had gone into Macedonia in search of Titus after failing to find him at Troas.

What the fightings and fears were is where the readings part. On the fightings there is rough agreement that they were external and violent, Barnes and Clarke both naming pagans, Jews and false brethren, Wesley naming the heathen alone, and Robertson and Ellicott declining to fix them, Ellicott suggesting either persecution from the heathen or conflict with the party of the circumcision at Philippi and admitting we have no knowledge. On the fears the divergence is sharper. Ellicott and Barnes make them Paul's own anxiety about the reception of his letter, and Clarke breaks that anxiety into its parts, lest the severity of the letter should alienate them, lest the party of the incestuous man should have prevailed, lest the false apostle should have perverted their minds. Wesley locates the source elsewhere, taking the fears to come from their brethren and to be fears lest these should be seduced. Calvin distinguishes the two by direction rather than by subject, the one being outward assaults from enemies and the other the anxiety caused by the internal maladies of the Church, since it was public rather than personal evils that disquieted him. Clarke closes the account with a remark none of the others make, that all was apprehension and the Spirit of God did not think proper to remove the causes of it in any extraordinary way.

The title given to God in the next verse is treated as more than a passing epithet. Ellicott observes that Paul's own experience seems to present itself to him as an attribute of the divine character, and suspects an allusion in the word for cast down to a disparaging name others had used of him. Robertson traces the same word from its literal sense of low on the ground through low in condition to the abject, and quotes the judgment that humility as a sovereign grace is the creation of Christianity. Gill describes the persons meant as those humbled under the afflicting hand of God who have low apprehensions of themselves, and Calvin draws the inference he thinks most profitable, that the more we have been afflicted the greater the consolation God has prepared, so that the epithet carries a promise. All then agree that the comfort came not chiefly from the reunion. Barnes notes that Paul had feared for Titus himself, perhaps that he was sick or dead, and that the greater joy was in the report; Calvin anticipates the objection that a friend's arrival would naturally cheer him and answers that it was the condition of the Corinthians and not the presence of one man; Ellicott specifies what in the report gave comfort, their longing, their uttered lamentation, and a zeal exercised not toward Paul but on his behalf against those who had slandered him.
8:
Chrysostom fastens on the exact form of the retraction. Paul does not say that he regretted before and does not now, but that he does not regret though he did; and the point of putting it that way, Chrysostom argues, is not to confess that the rebuke overshot but to heighten the praise. The amendment was so great that even supposing he had smitten them too severely and condemned himself for it, the result now justifies him. Robertson supplies the grammar behind the same observation, an imperfect in the concessive clause meaning he was in a regretful mood at first, and adds the lexical difficulty, that the verb here means to be sorry again and that we have transferred its sense to the word which properly means a change of mind. Ellicott locates the moment of regret, either on first hearing of their grief or during his earlier anxiety, when he had half wished he had not written so strongly, and prefers regret to repent as the rendering. Clarke states the same thing as experience: he had many doubts about the letter's success and grieved at having to write so severely, the case absolutely requiring it. Barnes guards the apostle further, holding that the word denotes only the uneasiness a good man feels from tenderness toward others, not from any consciousness of wrong, since what Paul wrote was right.

The distinction between being made sorry and repenting is where the commentators do their sharpest work. Robertson insists on it as a matter of language, that the sorrow is another form of regret or remorse while the second word means a change of mind and life, and that here the sorrow led to repentance and was not itself the repentance; he calls it a linguistic and theological tragedy that the one English word has to serve for the other. Ellicott says the true word is used here in the fulness of its meaning, and notes that the English variation between sorrowed and were made sorry answers to nothing in the Greek. On the qualifying phrase both press past the received rendering: Ellicott takes it literally as according to God, that is after his will and purpose, and Clarke supplies the practical test, that a man may sorrow and yet not repent, since this was not sorrow at being found out but sorrow at having sinned against God, which weighed with them more than any apprehension of punishment. Robertson reports another commentator's summary, that this is God's way as against man's way and the devil's.

Why severity was used at all is answered by two men reaching independently for the same image. Chrysostom compares little children who have undergone a painful remedy, an incision or a cautery or bitter physic, and are grateful afterwards; Calvin argues from the other side, that there are physicians good and faithful in other respects who are nonetheless harsh and do not spare their patients, and that Paul declares himself not of that disposition, employing harsh cures only under necessity. Calvin also explains why the letter had to be pitched as it was, since the discourse was addressed to a whole church in which some thought ill of him and some well, some were doubtful and some confident, some docile and some obstinate, so that he seems almost to sustain different characters as he turns from one to another. Gill keeps the feeling in view, that their grief as a natural passion gave him no pleasure and so far as it pained them it pained him too. Ellicott and Clarke both name what was avoided by the pain: on Ellicott's reading they were grieved so that they might sustain no loss, as they would have done had he held his peace, and on Clarke's their repentance spared him the exercise of an apostolic duty that would have gone hard with them.
10:
On what makes the sorrow godly the definitions divide between its author, its object and its measure. Gill traces it to its source, denying that it springs from free will, natural conscience, the law's work or fear of hell, and making it a gift of grace and the produce of almighty power, heightened by views of pardoning mercy and attended with faith. Calvin defines it by contrast with worldly sorrow, which is despondency under earthly affliction, whereas this has an eye to God and reckons the one misery to be the loss of his favour; and he makes it the cause and origin of repentance, since a man who is not dissatisfied with himself will never betake himself to the Lord. Barnes builds the definition out of the phrase itself, as sorrow according with God's own view of sin, arising when our estimate of its evil and ill desert answers to his. Clarke states it most compactly, that this sorrow has the breach of God's holy law for its object and cannot rest until it finds pardon. Ellicott objects meanwhile to the English rendering, calling needless variation the besetting sin of the version, and prefers throughout the sorrow that is after the will of God.

Two grammarians then disagree outright about what the qualifying adjective attaches to. Ellicott holds that it may govern either the repentance or the salvation and that the latter seems preferable; Robertson says flatly that it agrees with the repentance and not with the salvation, and adds that the word is an old verbal adjective found here alone in the New Testament. Both agree the English effaces something, Ellicott preferring a repentance giving no matter for regret, and Robertson observing that this clause by itself should have prevented the confusion between sorrow and change of life. On the contrasting sorrow of the world they converge from different directions. Robertson calls it grief for failure and not for sin, and instances Cain, Esau with his tears, and Judas; Ellicott says it leads only to remorse and despair, to the death of a broken heart, possibly to suicide, and in any case to the loss of eternal life. Clarke makes the same point from ordinary experience, that grief over lost goods or dead relatives, when deep, breeds disease and often drives men to lay desperate hands on themselves; Wesley simply takes the death worked by it as temporal, spiritual and eternal at once.

The seven marks that follow are handled as a list to be walked through. Ellicott numbers them and pairs each with what it replaced, earnestness where there had been indifference or even approval, the vindication sent through Titus, indignation against the offender, fear both of the threatened chastisement and of God's judgment, longing to have Paul among them again, new zeal for purity, and the sentence actually passed. Wesley sorts them instead by direction, apology and indignation with respect to themselves, fear and desire with respect to the apostle, zeal and revenge with respect to the offender, and calls the last a kind of holy revenge taken upon themselves by men scarcely able to forgive themselves. Calvin declines to argue whether these are effects of repentance or parts of it, and defines the first as an eager and active assiduity in correcting what is amiss, set against the drowsiness that lies inactive while sin is unfelt; he insists too that the clearing meant here consists rather in supplication for pardon than in extenuation of sin. Barnes reads the same word as diligence in removing the evil, noting that they neither sat down to mourn nor waited for God to remove it. Clarke keeps the distinction exact, that the Corinthians were not clear of blame in the matter itself, only in their efforts to rectify it.
12:
Who the injured party was is disputed at length. Clarke sets out four candidates, Paul himself, the church at Corinth, the offender's family and his father, and observes that taking it of the father would imply he was still living, which makes the transgression more flagrant, though the words might equally be spoken of a dead man whose injured honour cried from the earth like Abel's blood. Barnes decides for the father and thinks the passage evidence that he was alive when Paul wrote. Ellicott dismisses the alternatives sharply, calling any reading that makes the apostle or the community the injured party fantastic, and then presses the difficulty of how a father could be wronged at all: the union was a marriage and could only have been one if the first had been dissolved by divorce, and a man who had divorced his own wife could hardly claim to have suffered a wrong he had brought on himself; so Ellicott supposes the wife had divorced herself, a power wives held under Roman law and used with such licence that a satirist could speak of one who had eight husbands in five autumns.

On what the letter was really for the voices agree while differing over the text itself. Henry, Wesley, Barnes and Clarke all take the clause as Paul saying his concern was for the whole church, not principally for the wrongdoer nor merely for the redress of the man injured, since discipline is administered with a view to the welfare of the body. Robertson reads the Greek the other way. On his account the correct text is not our care for you but your earnest care for us, the two pronouns being easily interchanged; so the clause states what the letter was to bring to light in them rather than what it was to demonstrate in Paul. Calvin takes the following clause as the point of it, that the Corinthians showed by clear evidence that they had no part in the crime with which their connivance had seemed to connect them; and he is careful how far the acquittal reaches, palliating rather than clearing them, since their undue forbearance was not free from blame, and acquitting the body of the church rather than every member, since some had certainly countenanced it though the disgrace fell on all.

That Paul should rejoice chiefly over Titus rather than over them looks like a slight, and Chrysostom raises the objection himself before answering it: rejoicing for another man is no sign of loving these exceedingly, unless the joy was on their account, which is why the reason follows. He notices too that the text does not say Titus was refreshed but that his heart was, meaning his love for them. Ellicott recovers the sentence structure from the tense, so that Paul has been comforted and over and above that comfort rejoiced the more at another's joy, and he explains the sympathy behind it, that a man of that temper would have shared his delegate's disappointment and now shares his gladness. Robertson notes the doubled comparative as an ordinary idiom of the period, and that the joy of Titus rests on his being proud of what his labours had achieved. Calvin identifies what their comfort actually consisted in, that having acknowledged the fault they did not merely take the reproof in good part but received it joyfully, since the bitterness of a reproof is sweetened as soon as its profit begins to be tasted. Gill draws the general rule, that the flourishing condition of churches yields great consolation to their ministers.
14:
The boast Paul had made to Titus beforehand is filled in differently by each. Robertson supplies the circumstance, that Titus had hesitated to go at all after the failure of Timothy's mission, and was assured the Corinthians were sound at bottom and would come round if handled properly. Barnes guesses at the content, that he had told Titus they would receive him kindly and comply with his directions, and perhaps had spoken already of what they would give toward the collection. Gill lists the heads of the boast as their faith, their liberality, their affection and their obedience as children to a father. Clarke sets it in time, that the high character had been true before the false teacher got among them and changed their conduct, and that in returning to themselves they had made it true again. Robertson notices what makes the claim awkward and answers it: the same letter that boasted of them spoke plainly of their sins, and the two were not inconsistent, as the outcome proved. Ellicott handles a variant here, since some good manuscripts read your boasting rather than ours, making the sense that what they said of themselves proved as true as what Paul said of them; he prefers the received text as giving the better sense.

The word rendered inward affection draws comment from nearly everyone, and the comment is mostly about English. Ellicott says the margin gives the literal sense and that heart or feelings would serve best; Barnes and Calvin both explain that the Greek names the viscera and came to stand for the seat of the emotions, so that it denotes compassion, love and every tender affection. Calvin adds a purpose behind the report, that in describing Titus as thus moved Paul is working him into the affections of the Corinthians, since it is an advantage that the servants of Christ should be loved. Clarke calls the sentence a very natural picture, representing Titus as overjoyed even while delivering his account, and gives three reasons for his attachment, that they had loved the apostle, that they had shown kindness to himself, and that he found excellent gifts joined to humility. On their receiving him with fear and trembling, Ellicott takes it that Titus met not the petulant resistance he had feared but respectful reverence; Robertson calls the obedience of them all a remarkable statement of complete victory in spite of a stubborn minority still opposing Paul, and recalls that Paul himself had first come to Corinth in nervous dread.

The closing sentence is read as both a conclusion and a hinge. Ellicott corrects the rendering, noting that the better manuscripts omit the connecting word and that the phrase does not mean I trust you but I am of good cheer, I take courage in you being what you are; and he supposes that with this expression of thankfulness Paul leaves the painful subject, probably after a pause, and turns to another. Robertson puts it in three words, that the outcome has brought Paul joy, courage and hope. Gill and Barnes both see the verse doing work for what follows, Gill observing that it is meant partly to commend their past conduct and partly to pave the way for the request about the collection for the poor saints, and Barnes reporting the judgment that the whole address is wonderfully adapted to introduce that subject. Clarke widens the frame, arguing that the affair had threatened to ruin the church not at Corinth only but through all Greece, since had the man who denied the resurrection and opposed the apostle's authority prevailed there, his influence might have spread over Asia Minor too; which alone, he says, accounts for the depth of Paul's anxiety. Calvin draws the character lesson, that reproving to their face those you love while still hoping well of them is the signal evidence of a candid mind.
